input.topicDescription: B-tree indexes, selectivity, and write amplification.
input.projectGoal: Design schemas for a production Postgres app

questions.prompt: A query filters on a column with only two distinct values across ten million rows. Why might Postgres ignore a B-tree index on that column?

options.text: The index is too large to fit in memory
Low selectivity means a sequential scan is cheaper than many random reads
B-tree indexes cannot be built on low-cardinality columns
The planner only uses indexes on primary keys

questions.explanation: When a predicate matches a large fraction of the table, following index pointers costs more random I/O than reading the heap sequentially, so the planner picks the sequential scan.

questions.prompt: Adding an index to a table makes writes to that table slower.
questions.explanation: Every insert, update, and delete must maintain each index on the table, so write cost grows with the number of indexes.

questions.prompt: Name the Postgres system view you would query to find indexes that have never been scanned.
questions.explanation: pg_stat_user_indexes exposes idx_scan per index; a count of zero since the last stats reset means the index is unused.

questions.prompt: You have a composite index on (tenant_id, created_at). Which query can use it for both filtering and ordering?
questions.explanation: A composite index is usable left-to-right: fixing tenant_id leaves created_at already sorted within that prefix.

practiceSet.title: Database indexes: cost and selectivity
practiceSet.description: Four questions on when Postgres uses an index and what it costs.
